questions.question: In formal syllogism logic, what does the statement "Some A are B" guarantee?
options: At least one A is B, and definitely not all A are B
At least one A is B — it is still possible that all A are B
questions.rationale: "Some" only guarantees "at least one" in formal logic — it does not exclude the possibility that all A are B. Reading it as "not all" is one of the most common syllogism mistakes.

questions.question: If both given statements in a syllogism are of the form "Some A are B" and "Some B are C", what can be concluded about A and C?
questions.rationale: At least one universal (All/No) premise is required for any definite conclusion. Two particular ("Some") premises can combine in too many different Venn arrangements to guarantee anything about A and C.

questions.question: Statements: No teachers are students. All students are learners. Which conclusion definitely follows?
questions.rationale: Since all students are learners, and no teacher is a student, the student-learners are guaranteed not to be teachers — so at least some learners are not teachers.

questions.question: Two conclusions are: "All books are papers" and "Some books are not papers." What does the complementary pairs rule tell you about them?
options: At least one of the two must be true
questions.rationale: These two conclusions form a complementary pair — across every possible Venn arrangement, at least one of them must hold, so the answer always includes 'either I or II follows.'
